body_markdown:
For sonographers and clinicians, ultrasound is among their most effective tools. It is used for abdominal imaging, breast and thyroid evaluation, musculoskeletal care, vascular studies, and interventional procedures. Its portability, lack of ionizing radiation, and ability to provide real-time insight at the bedside make it invaluable.


And yet, demand is rising while the workforce remains.12 At the same time, differences in operator experience can affect image quality, measurements and reproducibility, creating challenges for consistent examinations.


These pressures carry into modern clinical practice, where imaging workflows are increasingly complex and time-sensitive. Clinicians must balance precision with efficiency. A clinician may need to identify anatomy, optimize images, take measurements, compare prior studies, document findings and complete a report during a tightly scheduled list. Artificial intelligence offers a way to streamline parts of this workload, but its integration introduces new challenges. These include automated segmentation, image reconstruction enhancement, anomaly detection, workflow optimization, and decision-support models. They may run on the device itself, on a nearby computer, within a hospital network, or in the cloud.


**Opening a traditionally closed system**


For decades, the ultrasound scanner was built as a self-contained instrument. Its software, processing power and clinical applications were engineered as part of the device, then validated and released together. That model supported reliability, but it also made the system difficult to extend. Adding a new algorithm often meant adapting it to the scanner’s proprietary architecture, repeating technical integration work and waiting for a future product release.


Applications may now be developed by universities, specialist software companies, health systems or equipment manufacturers. Some require access to live images. Others depend on acquired raw data or volumetric data, or computing resources beyond what can reasonably be placed inside the scanner. A system designed to run only vendor-installed software can make each new connection a custom project.


The LOGIQTM open platform addresses this problem through application programming interfaces, or APIs. These are defined, controlled pathways through which the scanner and another application can exchange information. An API may allow an algorithm to receive ultrasound data, return an analysis to the console or make software running elsewhere in the health system accessible during the examination.


The platform supports four integration models: applications hosted on the scanner; web applications accessed from the console but running in the cloud or on a hospital network; data-streaming applications that process live ultrasound data externally and return results during the exam; and advanced data collection for clinicians and researchers. Together, these options can make the system more adaptable without requiring every application to be rebuilt inside the device.


**At the point of scanning: hosted & web-based applications for faster clinical insights**


During a breast or thyroid examination, the sonographer is already balancing image acquisition, measurements, comparison with prior studies and documentation. When decision-support software sits on a separate workstation, using it can require extra transfers, duplicate data entry or a break in concentration. Hosted applications address that problem by running on the ultrasound console. These applications might be developed by GE HealthCare or by a third party that has completed its own regulatory process. Integration through the open platform can help keep the application within the existing examination workflow and can help reduce the technical work needed to bring a cleared product onto the system.


For example, **PIUR tUS inside**3 is a software application used as hosted app on LOGIQ that converts standard 2D ultrasound sweeps into a three-dimensional representation of the thyroid, enabling clinicians to visualize anatomy in multiple planes and perform consistent volumetric assessment. Automated segmentation helps outline nodules and supports volume measurement, follow-up and comparison over time, streamlining the overall workflow efficiency.


The Koios DS™4 application hosted on LOGIQ takes a different approach. Its breast and thyroid decision support applications use artificial intelligence to analyze lesion features and provide decision support for characterization (including AI cancer risk assessment), giving clinicians an additional analytical check while leaving the final interpretation in their hands.


Similarly, the DeepHealth Thyroid Suite5 offers thyroid nodule detection and characterization while helping streamline reporting and worksheet completion, including the ability to compare findings easily with prior examinations.


Advanced data collection is used for an ultrasound-based, AI-assisted prostate cancer diagnosis technology: **PCaVision**6 is a novel approach to diagnose prostate cancer by enabling instant 3D visualization of suspicious regions through heatmaps using advanced ultrasound technologies including 3D, CEUS and Shear Wave Elastography plus PCaVision analysis followed by targeted biopsy.


**Extending ultrasound to interventional care for advanced image-guided procedures**


B-mode is the conventional grayscale view used to visualize anatomy. When B-mode data is streamed from the scanner with very low delay, an external application can process or display the information during a procedure.


**MediView XR90**7 uses real-time ultrasound data for augmented reality planning and navigation in interventional procedures. Augmented reality places digital information within the operator’s view of the physical environment. The application can use the ultrasound image for procedural guidance without running entirely on the scanner. These advanced imaging technologies are designed to help enhance anatomical understanding, support procedural confidence, workflow efficiency, and facilitate collaboration within the interventional suite.


An open platform gives health systems more latitude to select tools that fit their protocols, staffing and reporting needs, while keeping those tools available at the console where the examination is performed.


**Accessing to the original ultrasound signal: advanced data collection for clinicians and researchers**


In everyday practice, the clinician sees a finished ultrasound image: a grayscale view of tissue, a color map of blood flow or a measurement placed on the screen. Before that image appears, the system has already processed the returning echoes through multiple stages, shaping the raw signal into something that can be interpreted quickly at the bedside.


For researchers, that finished image may leave important information out of reach. Radiofrequency, or RF, data sits much closer to the signal first captured by the probe. Access to it allows investigators to study new approaches to image formation, test signal-processing methods and develop algorithms using information that may be compressed or altered during conventional reconstruction.


The advanced data collection component of the LOGIQ open platform is designed to provide access to this underlying data for research. In practical terms, it gives investigators a way to work beneath the displayed image, where new methods for reconstruction, tissue characterization and algorithm development may begin to deliver better patient care.


**Advancing the next generation of imaging**


While LOGIQ’s open digital platform enables connectivity and scalability across the enterprise, its advanced imaging technologies bring that vision to life at the point of care, helping clinicians achieve consistent, high-quality images with greater ease and efficiency across a wide range of patients and clinical applications.


Across image formation, vascular assessment, liver evaluation and workflow automation, LOGIQ applications are designed to support more consistent examinations while reducing the number of manual steps required at the console. A few examples of applications that help fulfill this vision: cSound™ Imageformer is designed to maintain focus across the image and, together with XDclear™ transducers, to support technically challenging cases, including patients with a higher body mass index. Flow technologies such as color flow, Power Doppler, Microvascular Imaging with Radiant *flow* ™, B-Flow and Micro B-Flow allow clinicians to adjust vascular visualization to the anatomy and clinical question.


Quantitative liver tools add numerical information to the visual examination. Two-dimensional Shear Wave Elastography estimates tissue stiffness by measuring how mechanical waves move through the liver. UGAP evaluates ultrasound attenuation associated with liver fat, while UGFF estimates liver fat fraction. Hepatic Assistant combines 2D shear-wave elastography and UGFF in one workflow.


Automation can reduce repeated system interactions such as selecting presets, placing measurement calipers, adjusting color boxes and documenting anatomy. Auto Abdominal Color Assistant 2.0 delivered time savings of up to 46 percent and reduced system interactions by about two-thirds.8 With Scan Assistant, Auto Abdominal Suite 2.0 completed measurements up to 65 percent faster with 80 percent fewer system interactions.9 Without Scan Assistant, it reduced measurement and editing time by up to 44 percent and system interactions by 54 percent.10


EZ Imaging uses customizable probe presets and an updated touch panel. Compared with a traditional interface, it reduced setup time by 32 percent and required 38 percent fewer keystrokes.11 Compare Assistant places current and prior studies side by side in real time, while Raw Data allows post-exam adjustments to contrast, display, measurements and annotations.


**Working across the health system**


Health systems may operate ultrasound fleets across hospitals, outpatient centers and specialist departments. Presets, reporting, cybersecurity and equipment performance must remain consistent across those sites.


To enable this, VerisoundTM Fleet can connect to LOGIQ systems to support standardized system operations and preset management across the fleet. ViewPointTM Ultra introduces direct on-scanner reporting on LOGIQ in the United States. MyGEHealthCare provides performance indicators, Probe Check and remote service support system and transducer monitoring, and SonoDefense and eDelivery address cybersecurity and software distribution.


For clinicians, this can reduce interruptions and place relevant information within reach during the examination. Researchers can access image streams, volumetric data and raw ultrasound signals, while health systems can introduce new applications without rebuilding workflows around each one.


We live in a world where ultrasound teams are being asked to perform more complex examinations with limited time and uneven access to specialist expertise. It does not have to remain that way. With an open platform and AI powered features, LOGIQ can connect clinicians to the applications, data and computing resources they need, bringing useful innovation into the examination room while helping ultrasound remain timely, consistent and accessible.
